unit.unitTitle: I Think, I Hope, I Am Sure
unit.unitOverview: This unit is about saying what you think, and asking politely. You use I think, I hope and I am sure with a whole sentence after them. You join two ideas with so and when, and you ask with would and could. You also say what is not allowed, and put a short tag on the end to check.
unit.learningPath:
Lesson: hear an opinion, a polite request and a rule.
Words: four groups, thirty words for opinions, manners and rules.
Pattern 1: I think it closes at five.
Pattern 2: so for the result, when for the moment.
Pattern 3: mustn't, need, would and could.
Pattern 4: the tag on the end, down or up.
Reading: three texts, then nine questions with answers.
Speaking, writing, quiz, then the assignment.

visual.lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 10.
This unit is about what you think, and how you say it.
Start with the first pattern.
You take a short opening, then a whole sentence after it.
I think the shop closes at five.
I know the bus is late on Sunday.
I hope the office is still open.
I am sure this is the right form.
I believe she works on Tuesdays.
Look at the shape.
The opening is short: I think, I know, I hope, I am sure, I believe.
After it comes a whole sentence, with its own subject and its own verb.
The shop closes at five. That is a whole sentence on its own.
Put the opening in front of it and you have I think the shop closes at five.
You may put the word that in the middle.
I think that the shop closes at five.
Both are correct. Most people leave that out when they speak.
Now the negative, because English does something you may not expect.
We move the not to the front.
We do not usually say I think it is not open.
We say I do not think it is open.
It is softer, and it is what people say.
The second pattern joins two ideas.
Use so for the result.
The shop was closed, so I came back the next day.
The queue was long, so I waited outside.
Use when for the moment.
I pay when the machine is free.
When the door opens, please go in.
So answers the question why.
When answers the question at what moment.
Notice the comma.
If the when part comes first, put a comma after it.
When the door opens, please go in.
If it comes second, you need no comma.
Please go in when the door opens.
Now the third pattern.
Mustn't says a thing is not allowed.
You mustn't leave your bag in the corridor.
You mustn't use that machine yet.
Need says a thing is necessary.
You need a key card for this room.
I need to sign the form first.
And now the polite part.
Would and could make a request soft.
Could you open the window, please?
Would you mind waiting here?
I would like a copy of the form.
Can you open the window is correct English.
Could you open the window is the polite one.
At a desk, with somebody you do not know, choose could or would.
The fourth pattern is the small tag on the end.
You know the shape already: it is warm, isn't it?
Now listen to your voice.
If your voice goes down at the end, you are asking the person to agree.
The queue is slow, isn't it? You can both see that it is slow.
If your voice goes up at the end, you are really asking.
This is the right desk, isn't it? You are not sure, and you want an answer.
Same words, two jobs, and your voice decides which one.
The words of this unit are for opinions, for manners and for rules.
Believe, approve, disagree, suppose, imagine, doubt, insist, opinion.
Polite, rude, request, apologise, excuse, mind, bother, favour.
Warning, danger, escape, prevent, protect, strict, obey, ignore.
Therefore, however, although, besides, otherwise, anyway.
The opinions in this unit are small ones.
A bus route, a shop, an old machine that is broken.
You never have to take a side about anything larger than that.
The signs and the rules here are only examples of English.
They are not instructions about any real place.
In every task you may invent the person, the place and the time.
Now start with the words, then the four patterns.
Say every example out loud once before you write it.

readings.title: Two Views on the Number 12
readings.setting: A short page from a bus company, with two answers on it
readings.passageScript:
The number 12 bus runs every twenty minutes.
Last month the company asked people what they think of it. Here are two answers.

Ana, who takes it to work:
I think the number 12 is a good route. It is never very full, and the drivers are polite. However, it is slow after four o'clock. I am sure the problem is the roadworks, not the driver. I do not believe a new timetable will help. Therefore I would keep the route and mend the road.

Ben, who takes it on Saturdays:
I disagree. Twenty minutes is a long wait when it is cold. Although the drivers are kind, the bus is often late. I suppose the company knows this already. I doubt they will change anything, because a new bus costs a lot. Besides, nobody has asked us before this month.

The company replied to both. It thanked them, and it said this:
We have read every answer. We approve of the idea of mending the road, so we have asked about it. We cannot promise a new bus this year. When we know more, we will put a notice at every stop.

Two people, one bus, two opinions. Both of them gave a reason.

readings.title: How to Ask for Something at a Desk
readings.passageScript:
Every day you ask somebody for something. A form, a copy, a seat, a minute of their time. English has a soft way to do it, and it is worth learning.

The plain question is not wrong. Can you open the window? Everybody will understand it. But with a person you do not know, the soft way is better.

There are three steps.
First, say Excuse me. It tells the person you are about to speak.
Second, use could or would. Could you open the window, please? Would you mind moving your bag?
Third, say thank you, even for a small thing.

Two words often confuse people. If somebody asks Do you mind waiting? then no means it is fine. Mind means feel that something is a problem, so no problem means no.

Ask for a favour in the same shape. Could you do me a favour? Then say what it is.

If you must say sorry, apologise once and say what you will do next. A long excuse is not better than a short one.

It is also polite to say what you think, and to hear what the other person thinks. You can disagree without being rude. Say I see what you mean, then add but I think, and then give your reason.

None of this is about being quiet. It is about making a request easy to say yes to.

readings.title: Notice on the Wall of a Shared Workroom
readings.setting: A sheet of paper beside the door of a shared workroom
readings.passageScript:
THE SHARED WORKROOM: A NOTICE FOR EVERYONE WHO USES IT
This notice is an example of the English you see on a wall. It is not about any real room.

BEFORE YOU START
You need a key card to come in. Ask at the desk on the ground floor.
You mustn't prop the door open. It closes slowly, so give it a moment.

THE MACHINES
The big cutter has a yellow sticker on the side. A yellow sticker means danger.
You mustn't use the cutter until somebody has shown you how.
Wear the glasses on the hook. They protect your eyes from small pieces.
Keep the floor clear. This is to prevent a fall, not to make the room tidy.

BAGS AND COATS
Put bags in the cupboard, not in the corridor.
The rule about the corridor is strict, and the reason is simple: two people cannot pass.

IF SOMETHING GOES WRONG
Press the red button. It stops every machine in the room.
Then tell the person at the desk.
Do not ignore a strange sound. A small problem now is a large one later.

WHEN YOU LEAVE
Switch off at the wall. Take your work with you.
The room is checked at six.

If a rule here is not clear, ask at the desk. We would rather answer a question than write another notice.

I am sure. This is the right form. Together: I am sure this is the right form.
I believe. She works on Tuesdays. Together: I believe she works on Tuesdays.

with that, or without it
I think that the shop closes at five.
I think the shop closes at five.

the not moves to the front
Wrong: I think it is not open.
Right: I do not think it is open.
Wrong: I believe she is not coming.
Right: I do not believe she is coming.

hope is the one that keeps its own not
I hope it is not closed.

asking somebody else
Do you think it closes at five?
What do you think?
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
You have two pieces: I am sure, and the door is locked after six.
Step 1. Look at the second piece. Is it a whole sentence?
The door is locked after six. Yes. It has a subject and a verb.
Step 2. Put the opening in front of it, and add nothing else.
Answer: I am sure the door is locked after six.
Step 3. Now make it negative. The not goes to the front.
Answer: I am not sure the door is locked after six.
Say both out loud once.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to write I think it is not open. English usually moves the not to the front: I do not think it is open. The meaning is the same, and the second one is what people say.
grammar.memoryTip: The opening is short. What follows it is a whole sentence on its own.
grammar.practice:
Join the two pieces into one sentence.
1. I think. The shop closes at five.
2. I hope. The bus comes soon.
3. I am sure. This is the right desk.
4. I know. She works on Tuesdays.
5. I believe. The office opens at nine.
Now move the not to the front.
6. I think it is not open.
7. I believe she is not coming.
8. Write one sentence of your own that starts I am not sure.
grammar.answerKey:
1. I think the shop closes at five.
2. I hope the bus comes soon.
3. I am sure this is the right desk.
4. I know she works on Tuesdays.
5. I believe the office opens at nine.
6. I do not think it is open.
7. I do not believe she is coming.
Item 8 is your own writing, so there is no fixed answer. A model: I am not sure the machine is working.
The likeliest wrong answer is item 6. I think it is not open is not broken English, but it is rare. Move the not to the front and it sounds like a person.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: So for the result, when for the moment
grammar.explanation: Use so for the result: one thing happened, so another thing followed. Use when for the moment: one thing happens at the time of the other. Both join two whole sentences into one. Put a comma after the when part only when it comes first.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
so, for the result
The shop was closed, so I came back the next day.
The queue was long, so I waited outside.
I had no key card, so I asked at the desk.

when, for the moment
I pay when the machine is free.
She calls me when the post arrives.
I will sign it when I have read it.

the when part can come first, and then it takes a comma
When the door opens, please go in.
When the light is red, the machine is off.

no comma when it comes second
Please go in when the door opens.

the same two ideas, joined two ways
The bus was late. I walked.
The bus was late, so I walked.
I walked when the bus was late.
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
Two ideas: the office was full. I waited in the corridor.
Step 1. Ask why. Did the first idea cause the second? Yes, it did.
Step 2. A cause takes so, with a comma in front of it.
Answer: The office was full, so I waited in the corridor.
Step 3. Now the same two ideas with when.
When asks at what moment. The waiting happened at that time.
Answer: I waited in the corridor when the office was full.
Both are correct, and they say slightly different things.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to drop the comma before so: The office was full so I waited. English puts one there: The office was full, so I waited.
grammar.memoryTip: So answers why. When answers at what moment.
grammar.practice:
Write so or when in each gap.
1. The shop was closed, ... I came back later.
2. I always check the list ... I leave the house.
3. The queue was long, ... I waited outside.
4. Please ring the bell ... you arrive.
5. I had no ticket, ... I bought one at the machine.
Now two more.
6. Put the comma in the right place: When the door opens please go in.
7. Join these two ideas twice, once with so and once with when: The bus was late. I walked.
grammar.answerKey:
1. so  2. when  3. so  4. when  5. so
6. When the door opens, please go in.
7. The bus was late, so I walked. I walked when the bus was late.
Five out of five in items 1 to 5 means you have it. If you missed one, ask the gap a question: does it answer why, or at what moment?
The likeliest wrong answer is item 2. I check the list, so I leave the house says the list makes you leave, which is not what you mean.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: Mustn't, need, and the polite request
grammar.explanation: Mustn't says a thing is not allowed. Need says a thing is necessary. Would and could make a request soft, and that is what you use with a person you do not know. Can is correct too, but could is politer.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
mustn't: it is not allowed
You mustn't leave your bag in the corridor.
You mustn't use that machine yet.
We mustn't be late for the appointment.

need: it is necessary
You need a key card for this door.
I need to sign the form first.
She needs two copies, not one.

would and could: a soft request
Could you open the window, please?
Could I have a copy of this, please?
Would you mind waiting here?
I would like an appointment on Friday.

the answers you will hear
Yes, of course. Certainly. No, not at all.
No, I do not mind means it is fine.

plain and polite, side by side
Can you open the window?
Could you open the window, please?
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
You are at a desk, and you want a copy of a form.
Step 1. Say Excuse me first. It tells the person you are going to speak.
Step 2. Choose could or would, not can, because you do not know this person.
Step 3. Put please at the end.
Answer: Excuse me. Could I have a copy of this form, please?
Now the other side. The desk has a rule about the corridor.
Step 4. Not allowed takes mustn't.
Answer: You mustn't leave bags in the corridor.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to write You mustn't sign this when you mean it is necessary. Mustn't says do not do it. For necessary, use need: You need to sign this.
grammar.memoryTip: Mustn't shuts a door. Need opens one. Could and would knock first.
grammar.practice:
Choose the better word.
1. Excuse me. ... you open the window, please? (Can / Could)
2. You ... use that machine until somebody shows you. (mustn't / need)
3. I ... a key card for the door upstairs. (mustn't / need)
4. ... you mind waiting two minutes? (Would / Must)
5. I ... like an appointment on Friday, please. (would / must)
Now write.
6. Make this polite: Give me a form.
7. Make this a rule: bags in the corridor.
8. Answer this politely: Do you mind if I sit here?
grammar.answerKey:
1. Could  2. mustn't  3. need  4. Would  5. would
6. Excuse me. Could I have a form, please?
7. You mustn't leave bags in the corridor.
8. No, not at all. Or: No, I do not mind. Please sit down.
Item 8 catches people out. Mind means feel that something is a problem, so no is the friendly answer.
The likeliest wrong answer is item 2. Need would make it necessary to use the machine, which is the opposite of the rule.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: The tag that agrees, and the tag that really asks
grammar.explanation: A tag is the short question on the end. The same tag does two jobs, and your voice decides which. If your voice goes down, you are asking the person to agree. If it goes up, you are really asking, because you are not sure.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
your voice goes down: you want the person to agree
The queue is slow, isn't it?
That was a long wait, wasn't it?
It is cold in here, isn't it?
You both know it already. You are not asking for news.

your voice goes up: you are really asking
This is the right desk, isn't it?
You work on Fridays, don't you?
The office opens at nine, doesn't it?
You are not sure, and you want an answer.

the same words, two jobs
It is the last one, isn't it? Down: we can both see that.
It is the last one, isn't it? Up: please tell me.

what you say back
Yes, it is. No, it isn't. Yes, I do. No, I don't.
grammar.workedExample:
Here is one done for you.
You are at a counter, and you think it is the wrong one.
Step 1. Say the sentence you believe: This is the right counter.
Step 2. The sentence is positive, so the tag is negative: isn't it?
Step 3. You are not sure, so let your voice go up at the end.
Answer: This is the right counter, isn't it?
Now the other job. You and the person beside you are both waiting.
Step 4. Say it with your voice going down: It is slow today, isn't it?
Record both and listen. Your voice should rise once and fall once.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to put a positive tag on a positive sentence: It is warm, is it? English swaps it over: It is warm, isn't it?
grammar.memoryTip: Voice down, you want a yes. Voice up, you want an answer.
grammar.practice:
Add the tag, then write D for down or U for up.
1. You work on Fridays, ...? You are not sure.
2. That was a long wait, ...? You both waited.
3. It isn't far, ...? You are not sure.
4. She signed it, ...? You saw her sign it.
5. You don't mind, ...? You are not sure.
Now say it.
6. Say items 1 and 2 out loud and record them.
7. Write one sentence with a tag that you would really use tomorrow.
grammar.answerKey:
1. don't you? U
2. wasn't it? D
3. is it? U
4. didn't she? D
5. do you? U
Item 6: play the recording back. Item 1 should end higher than item 2. If both sound the same, say item 2 again slowly, with your voice falling on the last word.
Item 7 is your own writing, so there is no fixed answer. A model: This is the last form, isn't it?
The likeliest wrong answer is item 3. The sentence is already negative, so the tag is positive: is it?

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — I Think, I Hope, I Am Sure
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Say each line out loud. Then record all six and play them back.
1. I think the shop closes at five.
2. I hope the office is still open.
3. I am sure this is the right form.
4. I know the bus is late on Sunday.
5. I do not think it is open yet.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — For It, or Against It?
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Press Listen and hear these five lines. After each one, say your answer out loud: is this person for the idea, or against it?
The idea is simple. A shop near the station wants to close at eight instead of six.
1. I think a later closing time would help a lot of people.
2. I doubt anybody would come at eight at night.
3. I am sure the staff would be glad of the extra hours.
4. The shop is quiet after six already, however.
5. I approve of the plan, although it will cost something.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Asking at a Desk
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
You are at a desk, and you want four things. Say each request out loud, then record all four.
1. A copy of a form: Excuse me. Could I have a copy of this form, please?
2. A seat: Excuse me. Would you mind if I sit here?
3. An appointment: I would like an appointment on Friday, please.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Down for Agreement, Up for a Question
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Say each line twice. First with your voice going down at the end, then with your voice going up.
1. This is the right desk, isn't it?
2. It is slow today, isn't it?
3. You work on Fridays, don't you?
4. It isn't far, is it?
Record both versions of line 1 and play them back.
Down means you already know, and you want the other person to agree.
Up means you are not sure, and you want an answer.

speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Say four sentences with a tag, and tell me each time whether my voice went up or down.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — One Minute, One Opinion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Talk for one minute about one small question. Pick one of these three.
Should the shop near you open later?
Is the bus route you take a good one?
Is an old machine worth mending?
Use this shape.
Say what you think: I think ...
Give a reason: ... because ...
Give the other side: However, ...
Finish: So on balance, I think ...
Record the minute and play it back.
Check yourself. Count three things: one I think, one reason, one however.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Start It, Keep It Going, Finish It
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
A short exchange has three parts. Practise all three.
Start it: Excuse me. Could I ask you something?
Keep it going: I see. And do you think it is the same on Saturdays?
Finish it: That is very helpful. Thank you.

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 1 — Two Paragraphs About a Bus Route
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write two short paragraphs about a bus route. You may invent the route, the times and the town.
Paragraph 1: what is good about it.
Paragraph 2: what is not good about it.
Use so once, when once and however once.
Leave one empty line between the two paragraphs.
writing.modelText:
The number 12 comes every twenty minutes. It is never full in the morning, so I always get a seat. I read when the road is quiet.

However, it is slow after four. The road is being mended, so every bus waits at the corner. I walk home when the wait is longer than ten minutes.
writing.successCriteria: Two paragraphs. Six sentences in all. One so, one when and one however. A capital letter and a full stop in every sentence. One empty line between the paragraphs.
writing.support: Write the six sentences first, in any order. Then put the three good ones together and the three not-good ones together. Only then add so, when and however.
writing.extension: Add a third paragraph of one sentence. Start it with Therefore, and say what you would change.

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 2 — A Polite Note
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short note that asks for two things. You may invent the person and the place.
Ask for a copy of a form, and ask for an appointment.
Use could once and would once.
Say thank you at the end.
writing.modelText:
Dear Ana,
Could I have a copy of the form for the workroom key, please?
I would also like an appointment on Friday afternoon, if that is possible.
I am sorry to bother you twice in one week.
Thank you very much.
Ben
writing.successCriteria: Five or six lines. One could. One would. One thank you. A capital letter at the start of every line.
writing.support: Write the two requests first as plain questions. Then put Could I or Would you in front of each one, and please at the end.
writing.extension: Add one line that apologises for a small thing. Keep it to one sentence, with no long excuse.

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 3 — What I Think, and Why
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write four sentences giving your opinion about one small thing.
Pick one: an old machine that is broken, a shop that shuts early, a route you take.
Sentence 1 starts I think.
Sentence 2 gives a reason.
Sentence 3 starts I am not sure, or I doubt.
Sentence 4 starts I hope.
writing.modelText:
I think the old kettle is worth mending.
It is heavy and well made, and a new one costs more than the repair.
I am not sure the shop still sells the part.
I hope somebody there can tell me on Saturday.
writing.successCriteria: Four sentences. One starts I think. One starts I am not sure or I doubt. One starts I hope. Every sentence has a capital letter and a full stop.
writing.support: Write the four plain facts first, with no opening at all. Then put I think, I am not sure and I hope in front of three of them.
writing.extension: Rewrite sentence 3 with the not at the front, like this: I do not think ...

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 4 — A Short Notice
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short notice for a shared room. You may invent the room.
Give it a heading in capital letters, then four lines under it.
Two lines say what is not allowed, with mustn't.
One line says what is necessary, with need.
One line says who to ask.
This is an example of English, not a rule for any real place.
writing.modelText:
THE SHARED KITCHEN
You mustn't leave plates in the sink.
You mustn't move somebody else's food.
You need a key card for the door after seven.
If something is broken, ask at the desk.
writing.successCriteria: A heading in capital letters. Four lines under it. Two lines with mustn't. One line with need. One line saying who to ask.
writing.support: Write the four plain sentences first. Then put You mustn't in front of the two that are not allowed.
writing.extension: Add one more line that gives the reason for one rule, joined with so.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 1 — So, When and the Joining Words
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Part A. Write so or when in each gap.
1. The road was closed, ... I walked.
2. I read the notice ... I arrive.
3. Nobody answered, ... I left a note.
4. She signs the form ... the desk is free.
5. There was no key card, ... I waited outside.
6. Please press the button ... the light is green.
Part B. Choose the best joining word: therefore, however, although, besides, otherwise, anyway.
7. It is cheap. ..., it takes an hour.
8. The form was wrong. ... it came back.
9. ... it was cold, the queue was long.
10. I do not want it. ..., it costs too much.
11. Sign it today, ... it comes back.
12. The bus was late, but I walked ... .
activities.answerSummary:
Part A: 1. so  2. when  3. so  4. when  5. so  6. when
Part B: 7. However  8. Therefore  9. Although  10. Besides  11. otherwise  12. anyway
Twelve out of twelve means you have it.
Nine to eleven means check the ones you missed, one question each: does it give a reason, a difference, an extra reason or a warning?
Eight or fewer means read Pattern 2 again before you go on.
activities.soloPath: Do it in writing, then read every finished sentence out loud. Your ear will catch a wrong one that your eye missed.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 2 — Choose the Opening
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Choose I think, I hope, I am sure or I doubt for each one.
1. You looked at the sign two minutes ago. ... the shop closes at five.
2. You have no information at all, but you want it to be true. ... the bus comes soon.
3. It is nine at night. ... anybody is still at the desk.
4. You saw her here last Tuesday. ... she works on Tuesdays.
5. Nobody has answered your note for a week. ... they read it.
6. You want the weather to be dry tomorrow. ... it stays dry.
7. Make item 3 into a sentence that starts I do not think.
8. Write one sentence of your own with I am sure.
activities.answerSummary:
1. I am sure  2. I hope  3. I doubt  4. I think  5. I doubt  6. I hope
7. I do not think anybody is still at the desk.
Item 8 is your own writing, so there is no fixed answer. A model: I am sure this is the right building.
Six or more of the first six means you have it.
Items 1 and 4 are the pair to watch. I am sure is for something you have just checked. I think is for something you believe but have not checked today.
activities.soloPath: Say each finished sentence out loud before you write it. The opening you would really say is usually the right one.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 3 — Say It Politely
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Rewrite each line so that a person you do not know would be happy to hear it.
Use Excuse me, could, would and please.
1. Give me a form.
2. Open the window.
3. Move your bag.
4. I want an appointment on Friday.
5. Hold this.
6. Tell me where the desk is.
7. Wait here.
8. Answer this politely: Do you mind if I sit here?
activities.answerSummary:
There is more than one good answer. These are models.
1. Excuse me. Could I have a form, please?
2. Could you open the window, please?
3. Would you mind moving your bag?
4. I would like an appointment on Friday, please.
5. Could you do me a favour and hold this?
6. Excuse me. Could you tell me where the desk is?
7. Would you mind waiting here?
8. No, not at all. Please sit down.
Six or more with could, would or please in them means you have it.
Item 8 is the one people miss. Mind means feel that something is a problem, so the friendly answer is no.
activities.soloPath: Read your version and the model out loud, one after the other. If yours is shorter than the model, check that please or could is still in it.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 4 — Mustn't or Need
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write mustn't or need in each gap.
1. You ... a key card for this door.
2. You ... prop the door open.
3. I ... to sign the form first.
4. You ... use the cutter until somebody shows you.
5. She ... two copies, not one.
6. We ... be late for the appointment.
7. You ... leave bags in the corridor.
8. I ... a copy of this for the desk.
activities.answerSummary:
1. need  2. mustn't  3. need  4. mustn't  5. needs  6. mustn't  7. mustn't  8. need
Eight out of eight means you have it.
Six or seven means check the ones you missed with one question: is it not allowed, or is it necessary?
Item 5 is the one to watch. She takes needs, with an s on the end.
activities.soloPath: After you write each answer, say the whole sentence out loud and ask yourself: am I forbidding this, or am I saying it is necessary?

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 5 — Add the Tag
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Add the tag to each sentence.
1. It is warm in here, ...?
2. You work on Fridays, ...?
3. It isn't far, ...?
4. She signed it, ...?
5. You don't mind, ...?
6. He didn't call, ...?
7. They are strict about bags, ...?
8. Mark items 1 to 7 with D if you would say them with your voice going down, or U if you are really asking.
activities.answerSummary:
1. isn't it?  2. don't you?  3. is it?  4. didn't she?  5. do you?  6. did he?  7. aren't they?
Six or more of the first seven means you have it.
Item 8 has no fixed answer, because it depends on what you already know. The rule is simple: D if you and the other person can both see it, U if you are not sure.
The ones to watch are 3, 5 and 6. The sentence is already negative, so the tag is positive.
activities.soloPath: Say each finished sentence out loud twice, once falling and once rising. The one that sounds natural to you is the one you would really use.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 6 — Finding It in the Notice
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Look at the notice on the wall of the shared workroom. Answer in a few words.
1. What do you need before you can come in?
2. Where do you ask for it?
3. Name one thing the notice says you mustn't do.
4. Why must the floor be kept clear?
5. What does the red button do?
6. What time is the room checked?
activities.answerSummary:
1. A key card.
2. At the desk on the ground floor.
3. Prop the door open. Or: use the cutter before somebody shows you. Or: leave bags in the corridor.
4. To prevent a fall.
5. It stops every machine in the room.
6. At six.
Five or six right means you can find what you need in a notice.

assignments.title: What I Think: a spoken opinion and a written note
assignments.instructions:
This assignment has two parts. You may invent every fact in it.

Part 1, spoken.
Record ninety seconds about one small question.
Pick one: a shop's closing time, a bus route, or an old machine that is broken.
Say what you think, give a reason, give the other side with however, and finish.
Use one tag question somewhere, and say it the way you really mean it.

Part 2, written.
Write a short note of five or six lines to the person who decides.
Ask for one thing politely, with could or would.
Give your opinion in one sentence that starts I think.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: The commonest error in this unit is I think it is not open. It is not a vocabulary problem and it is not careless. The learner has built the sentence in the order the meaning arrives, and English happens to move the not forward. Do not name a rule. Put the two lines side by side, I think it is not open and I do not think it is open, and ask which one the learner has heard people say. Almost everybody chooses the second, and then the correction is theirs rather than yours.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: Pattern 4 is the only part of this unit that cannot be checked on paper. The words of a tag are easy and the voice is the whole lesson, so a learner can get every written item right and still say both versions the same way. Speaking 4 asks for two recordings of one line for exactly that reason. Listen for the last word: it should fall once and climb once. If the two recordings match, the learner has not yet heard the difference, and repeating the written practice will not help.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: Every opinion in this unit is a small one on purpose: a bus route, a shop's closing time, whether an old machine is worth mending. No task asks the learner to take a side on anything larger, and none asks about their home, their work, their money or their health. The signs and rules in Reading 3 and Writing 4 are examples of the English that appears on a wall, and the notice says so in its own second line. If a learner brings a real situation of their own, keep the work on the English.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: Two items turn on the same point and are worth looking at together: Pattern 3 item 8 and Practice 3 item 8, both Do you mind if I sit here? Mind means feel that something is a problem, so the friendly answer is no. Learners who answer yes have understood the words and not the direction. The quickest repair is to replace mind with is it a problem and read the exchange again.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: A learner who finishes early can redo Speaking 5 with the other side first, which is harder, or turn Writing 1 into three paragraphs by adding a Therefore sentence. A learner who is finding it heavy should do Pattern 1 and Practice 2 on one day and leave the tags until the next. The four patterns do not depend on each other, so they can be taken in any order and spread across four short sittings.
